---
title: "Comparing the stockpile with SAG"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5
)
options(width = 100)
```

The official results of an ICES stock assessment are the summary tables in the
ICES Stock Assessment Graphs database, [SAG](https://sg.ices.dk): spawning
stock biomass, fishing pressure, recruitment and catches by year. The
stockpile holds the detail behind those tables, the numbers, weights,
maturity and mortality by age. If a submitted stock object really is the
assessment that the advice was based on, the summary calculated from it should
be the same as the summary in SAG.

This article makes that comparison, for one stock and then for all of them,
using the [icesSAG](https://github.com/ices-tools-prod/icesSAG) package to
read SAG and the [FLCore](https://flr-project.org) package to calculate the
summary. It is run against the live SAG database each time this site is built,
so the results change as assessments are published or corrected.

```{r}
library(FLStockpile)
library(FLCore)
library(icesSAG)
library(ggplot2)

options(FLStockpile.url = "https://github.com/neilcampbelll/FLstockpile/releases/download/v2026.001")
```

## Summary of a stock

The summary of a stock in the stockpile is calculated from its `FLStock`
object. The spawning stock biomass, mean fishing mortality and recruitment
come from the model estimates. The catches in SAG are usually the observed
catches, so the catches come from the observed data where the stockpile has
them, and from the estimates otherwise.

```{r}
# The summary of a stock assessment in the stockpile.
#
# Returns a data frame with one row per quantity and year.

stockpile_summary <- function(stock_code, assessment_year) {
  estimated <- stockpile_flstock(stock_code, assessment_year, type = "estimated")
  version <- stockpile_stocks(stock_code, assessment_year)
  catches <- if (version$observed) {
    catch(stockpile_flstock(stock_code, assessment_year, type = "observed"))
  } else {
    catch(estimated)
  }

  quantities <- list(SSB = ssb(estimated), F = fbar(estimated), recruitment = rec(estimated), catches = catches)
  rows <- lapply(names(quantities), function(quantity) {
    values <- as.data.frame(quantities[[quantity]])
    data.frame(quantity = quantity, year = values$year, stockpile = values$data)
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

# The summary of a stock assessment in SAG, in the same layout.

sag_summary <- function(stock_code, assessment_year) {
  sag <- getSAG(stock_code, assessment_year)
  rows <- lapply(c("SSB", "F", "recruitment", "catches"), function(quantity) {
    data.frame(quantity = quantity, year = sag$Year, sag = sag[[quantity]])
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

# The two summaries side by side, for the years and quantities in both.

compare_summaries <- function(stock_code, assessment_year) {
  both <- merge(stockpile_summary(stock_code, assessment_year), sag_summary(stock_code, assessment_year))
  both <- both[!is.na(both$stockpile) & !is.na(both$sag) & both$sag != 0, ]
  both$ratio <- both$stockpile / both$sag
  both[order(both$quantity, both$year), ]
}
```

## One stock

Sole in the eastern English Channel, `sol.27.7d`, has both observed data and
model estimates in the stockpile.

```{r}
sole <- compare_summaries("sol.27.7d", 2026)
tail(sole[sole$quantity == "SSB", ], 5)
tail(sole[sole$quantity == "catches", ], 5)
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Four panels, one each for catches, F, recruitment and SSB of sol.27.7d by year, with the SAG values as points and the stockpile values as a line."}
ggplot(sole, aes(year)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = sag, colour = "SAG")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = stockpile, colour = "stockpile")) +
  facet_wrap(~quantity, scales = "free_y") +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL, title = "sol.27.7d, assessment year 2026") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The largest difference, in any year, for each quantity:

```{r}
aggregate(ratio ~ quantity, sole, function(ratio) max(abs(ratio - 1)))
```

## All stocks

The same comparison is made for the latest version of every stock assessment
in the stockpile that has model estimates. Stocks with more than one season,
unit or area are left out, because their summary cannot be calculated in the
same simple way, and so are stocks that are not found in SAG.

```{r}
stocks <- stockpile_stocks()
stocks <- stocks[stocks$estimated, ]
stocks$simple <- stocks$n_seasons == 1 & stocks$n_units == 1 & stocks$n_areas == 1

comparisons <- lapply(which(stocks$simple), function(i) {
  compared <- try(compare_summaries(stocks$stock_code[i], stocks$assessment_year[i]), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(compared, "try-error") || nrow(compared) == 0) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  cbind(stock_code = stocks$stock_code[i], assessment_year = stocks$assessment_year[i], compared)
})
comparisons <- do.call(rbind, comparisons)

stocks$compared <- paste(stocks$stock_code, stocks$assessment_year) %in%
  paste(comparisons$stock_code, comparisons$assessment_year)
```

Of the `r nrow(stocks)` stock assessments with estimates, `r sum(stocks$compared)`
could be compared with SAG. Not compared because they have seasons, units or
areas: `r paste(unique(stocks$stock_code[!stocks$simple]), collapse = ", ")`.
Not found in SAG: `r paste(unique(stocks$stock_code[stocks$simple & !stocks$compared]), collapse = ", ")`.

A stock and quantity is taken to be the same in the stockpile and in SAG if
they are within 2.5% of each other in every year. SAG holds rounded values, so
small differences are expected: a fishing mortality of 0.02 held to three
decimal places can be 2.5% out.

```{r}
agreement <- aggregate(
  ratio ~ stock_code + assessment_year + quantity, comparisons,
  function(ratio) max(abs(ratio - 1)) < 0.025
)
names(agreement)[4] <- "same"

table(agreement$quantity, ifelse(agreement$same, "same", "different"))
```

```{r}
all_same <- aggregate(same ~ stock_code + assessment_year, agreement, all)
```

`r sum(all_same$same)` of the `r nrow(all_same)` stock assessments are the same
as SAG in every quantity that could be compared.

### Where they differ

For each stock and quantity that is not the same, the median over the years of
the stockpile value divided by the SAG value, and the range. A blank means the
quantity is the same, and `-` that it could not be compared.

```{r}
ratios <- aggregate(
  ratio ~ stock_code + assessment_year + quantity, comparisons,
  function(ratio) {
    if (max(abs(ratio - 1)) < 0.025) {
      ""
    } else {
      sprintf("%s (%s to %s)", signif(median(ratio), 3), signif(min(ratio), 3), signif(max(ratio), 3))
    }
  }
)
ratios <- reshape(ratios, idvar = c("stock_code", "assessment_year"), timevar = "quantity", direction = "wide")
names(ratios) <- sub("ratio.", "", names(ratios), fixed = TRUE)
ratios[is.na(ratios)] <- "-"
ratios <- ratios[rowSums(ratios[-(1:2)] != "" & ratios[-(1:2)] != "-") > 0, ]

knitr::kable(ratios[order(ratios$stock_code), ], row.names = FALSE)
```

There are several reasons for a difference, and most of them are not errors:

- **Catches.** The stockpile catches are the estimates where no observed data
  were submitted, and SAG usually has the observed catches. A median close to
  1 with a range around it is what that looks like.
- **Units.** SAG may hold a quantity in different units, for example
  recruitment in millions against thousands in the stock object, giving a
  ratio of 0.001 or 1000.
- **Relative quantities.** For some stocks SAG holds the biomass and fishing
  pressure relative to a reference point, such as B/B~MSY~, or a harvest rate
  in place of a fishing mortality. The description of each quantity is in the
  `stockSizeDescription` and `fishingPressureDescription` columns of
  `getSAG()`.
- **Definitions.** The spawning stock biomass or recruitment published may be
  defined differently from the standard calculation used here, for example at
  another time of year or at another age.
- **A different assessment.** If none of these apply, the submitted stock
  object may not be the assessment that was published.

The stocks compared, with how SAG describes their quantities:

```{r}
descriptions <- lapply(which(stocks$compared), function(i) {
  sag <- getSAG(stocks$stock_code[i], stocks$assessment_year[i])
  data.frame(
    stock_code = stocks$stock_code[i],
    assessment_year = stocks$assessment_year[i],
    stock_size = sag$stockSizeDescription[1],
    stock_size_units = sag$stockSizeUnits[1],
    fishing_pressure = sag$fishingPressureDescription[1],
    recruitment_age = sag$recruitment_age[1]
  )
})

knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, descriptions), row.names = FALSE)
```
